check:0:0.a:
"It's faster" misses the real problem. On the first deploy, a single stack doesn't run slowly. It can't plan at all.

Here's why. The `databricks` provider (the plugin Terraform uses to talk to Databricks) needs the workspace URL before it can do anything. Say a Service stage creates the workspace and also adds team-sales clusters from `clusters.yml`. On a brand-new environment, that URL doesn't exist yet. So the provider can't connect, and the plan fails before anything is built.

Is there any truth in "faster"? A little. Smaller stacks can plan and apply more quickly. But that's a side effect, not the reason for the split. On the first deploy, the two stacks run one after the other, so you don't save time overall.

The split works because of the **stack dependency**, which is a rule that one Spacelift stack runs only after another finishes. The first stack creates the workspace. The contents stack, with clusters and things like `sp-sales-etl-dev`, plans afterwards.

"The workspace URL exists by the time the second stack plans" is better because it names the actual blocker, and it explains why the contents stack can plan once the workspace stack has finished.

judge.notes: The lesson never says smaller stacks plan or apply faster, or that two stacks give no overall time saving, so the 'a little truth in faster' paragraph adds claims the lesson does not support.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Spacelift requires one stack per provider”?
check:0:2.a:
That option sounds plausible, but it isn't true. Spacelift has no rule like that. One stack can use several **providers** (plugins that let Terraform talk to a service). The Foundation stage, for example, could use both `azurerm` and `databricks` in the same code.

It does get one thing half right. In our split, the workspace stack is mostly `azurerm`, and the contents stack is mostly `databricks`. So the line between stacks happens to follow the providers.

But it misses *why* we split. The `databricks` provider needs the workspace URL to connect. On the very first deploy, that workspace doesn't exist yet. So a single stack can't even make its plan, because the provider has nowhere to connect. The problem is timing, not a Spacelift rule.

With two stacks and a **stack dependency** (a rule that one stack runs only after another finishes), the first stack creates the workspace. Then the second stack plans against a real workspace.

"The workspace URL exists by the time the second stack plans" is the better answer because it names the real cause: the provider needs a live workspace before it can plan.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that Spacelift has no one-stack-per-provider rule, and the remark that the stack split follows the providers, go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “It creates A first, then B”?
check:1:0.a:
"It creates A first, then B" gets one thing right. Terraform does create resources in order, each one after the things it needs.

But that order only works when something can go first. Here, A uses a value from B. So A can't be created until B exists. B uses a value from A. So B can't be created until A exists. Neither one can start.

Think of it like a Spacelift run where `azurerm_databricks_workspace.this` needed an ID from `databricks_metastore_assignment.this`, while the assignment also needed the workspace's `workspace_id`. Each is waiting on the other. There is no "first."

Terraform also doesn't guess or pick one at random. It builds its dependency graph during plan, before creating anything. A dependency graph is its map of which resource needs which one first. When that map has a loop, Terraform stops right there. Nothing gets created, so nothing is half-built in DEV.

"It stops with a Cycle error" is better because it matches what really happens: Terraform finds the loop at plan time and refuses to go on, rather than creating anything.

judge.notes: No real problems. The reverse dependency (workspace needing something from the metastore assignment) is invented, but it is clearly framed as a hypothetical. The answer is about 180 words.

check:1:2.q: Why not “It creates both at the same time”?
check:1:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Terraform *does* create resources at the same time when they don't need each other. Two clusters for `team-sales` with no links between them can be built side by side.

But here, A uses a value from B, and B uses a value from A. A value like an ID only exists after a resource is created. So A can't start until B is finished, and B can't start until A is finished. Building them "at the same time" doesn't help, because neither has the value it needs at the start.

Picture a `databricks_cluster` that needs the ID of `sp-sales-etl-dev`, while that service principal also needs the cluster's ID. There's no first step. It's like being told to put on shoes before socks *and* socks before shoes.

Terraform spots this loop in its dependency graph while planning. That is its map of what needs what first. It stops before creating anything, so you never get a half-built stack in Spacelift.

"It stops with a Cycle error" is better because it names what really happens: Terraform finds the loop at plan time, reports `Error: Cycle`, and builds nothing.

judge.notes: Minor: the parallel-creation point and the 'never a half-built stack in Spacelift' claim go slightly beyond the lesson, but neither contradicts it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “The container first, then the account”?
check:2:0.a:
This option gets one thing right. It sees that the two resources are linked, so Terraform can't create them in just any order.

But it gets the direction backwards. The container *uses* the account's name. That reference is how Terraform builds its dependency graph, the map of what needs what first. A reference points at something that must already exist. You can't write the account's name into the container before the account has been created.

Think socks before shoes. The shoes go on over the socks, so the socks come first. The container sits inside the account, so the account comes first.

Here is a setup a platform team might use for Unity Catalog storage in DEV:

```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "uc" {
  name = "stsalesucdev"
  # ...
}

resource "azurerm_storage_container" "uc" {
  name                 = "sales-catalog"
  storage_account_name = azurerm_storage_account.uc.name
}
```

The container points at `azurerm_storage_account.uc`. So Terraform waits for the account before it creates the container.

"The account first, then the container" is better because the thing being referred to must always exist before the thing that refers to it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Both at once, the order doesn't matter”?
check:2:1.a:
"Both at once" gets one thing right. A single `terraform apply` (the step that actually builds things) does create both. You don't need two separate runs.

What it misses is the **reference**. The container's code points at the account, like this:

```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_container" "sales" {
  name                 = "sales-dev"
  storage_account_name = azurerm_storage_account.sales.name
}
```

That line `azurerm_storage_account.sales.name` is a link from one resource to another. Terraform reads links like this and draws its **dependency graph**, a map of which resource needs which other one first. Here the map says the container needs the account.

It doesn't matter that the name is a plain value already set in the code. The reference alone is enough to set the order. Terraform always creates a resource after the ones it refers to. So the order does matter, and Terraform decides it for you.

"The account first, then the container" is better because it follows the link the container's reference creates in the dependency graph.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The answer says what 'both at once' gets right, explains the reference and dependency graph, and ends with a single-sentence reason the account-first answer is better.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Point the Databricks provider at the workspace …” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
The Databricks provider is the plug-in Terraform uses to talk to one workspace. It needs that workspace's URL, called its `host`.

If you paste the URL in by hand, two things go wrong. If the workspace is ever recreated, Azure gives it a new URL. Your code still points at the old one, so every cluster and grant fails. And when you add UAT or PROD, you must remember to change the URL. Forget once, and team-sales' DEV clusters land in the wrong workspace.

So take the URL from the workspace resource instead:

```hcl
provider "databricks" {
  host = azurerm_databricks_workspace.this.workspace_url
}
```

Now the URL always follows the real workspace.

There is one catch. In a brand-new environment the workspace doesn't exist yet. Its URL is unknown at plan time, so the provider can't plan. So the workspace goes in one Spacelift stack and its contents in another. The workspace stack outputs (shares) the URL. A stack dependency runs the contents stack only after that apply and passes the URL along.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Add whatever is ready next” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The problem (about 10 seconds)**
"In our workspace stack, `azurerm_databricks_workspace.this` needs its resource group and VNet first. The `databricks_metastore_assignment` needs the workspace's `workspace_id`. Terraform has to pick a safe order. It reads these references and builds a **dependency graph**, a map of what needs what first."

**The idea (about 10 seconds)**
"Add whatever is ready next. A resource is ready when everything it needs is already placed. Repeat until all are placed. It's like getting dressed: socks before shoes."

**Edge case (about 10 seconds)**
"If a round finds nothing ready, the leftovers are waiting on each other. That's a loop, and Terraform stops with `Error: Cycle`. Picking names A to Z each round keeps the order predictable. But it re-scans the list every round, so it's slower on big graphs."

**Likely follow-up:** "Why not put the workspace and its clusters and service principals in one stack?"

*Hint:* The Databricks provider needs a real workspace URL to plan. Before the workspace exists, it can't. So split them into two Spacelift stacks. Add a **stack dependency**, a rule that the contents stack runs only after the workspace stack applies.

judge.notes: The edge-case part says the method "re-scans the list every round, so it's slower on big graphs", which the lesson never says, and it presents the exercise's A-to-Z picking as if it were what Terraform does; the claim that the workspace needs a resource group and VNet is also not in the lesson.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Apply fails halfway with "not found" errors.** For example, `databricks_metastore_assignment` runs before the workspace exists. This usually means an ID was typed in as plain text instead of referring to the other resource. Terraform only waits for things it can see a reference to.
- **A rerun "fixes" it.** The first apply fails and the second succeeds. That points to an order Terraform never knew about.
- **`Error: Cycle` at plan time.** Two or more resources point at each other, so neither can go first. Look for references that run both ways between them.
- **The Service stack can't plan.** The Databricks provider (the plugin that talks to Databricks) has no workspace to connect to. This happens when the workspace and its contents sit in one stack, or when no stack dependency makes Service wait for the workspace stack.

**Quickest check**

Open the code for the failing resource. Is `workspace_id` written as a reference like `azurerm_databricks_workspace.this.workspace_id`, or as a typed-in value? Check the code, not the plan. A plan shows the final values, so it can't tell you which one was used.

Then, in Spacelift, confirm that the Service stack depends on the stack that creates the workspace.

judge.notes: The claim that a plan can't show whether workspace_id was a reference or a typed value is wrong and not in the lesson. A plan marks a reference to a not-yet-created resource as "known after apply", so the plan can reveal it.

learn:stops.a:
**When does "Terraform works out the order" stop working?**

**1. The dependency lives outside Terraform.**
Say a grant to `grp-sales-dev-owners` needs that group in Databricks. A separate sync process outside Terraform copies it in from Entra ID. Terraform can't see that process, so it can't wait for it, and `depends_on` only waits for resources Terraform manages. A `data` source (a read-only lookup of something that already exists) makes the plan stop with a clear error if the group isn't there yet. To truly fix the order, have Terraform create the group itself, or run the stack only after the sync has finished.

**2. A provider needs something that doesn't exist yet.**
The `databricks` provider needs a workspace URL to plan. On a first run in DEV, that workspace hasn't been created. Put the workspace in one Spacelift stack and its contents in another, linked by a stack dependency.

**3. Two resources point at each other.**
Suppose a cluster's settings refer to a policy, and the policy refers back to the cluster. Terraform reports `Error: Cycle`. Break the loop by moving one link into its own resource, such as a separate permissions resource.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Minor: `depends_on` and 'provider' are not explained, and 'depends_on only waits for resources Terraform manages' is slightly loose, but it does not contradict the lesson.

learn:term.a:
A **stack** is one set of Terraform code with its own state. State is the file where Terraform records what it has built. Spacelift plans and applies each stack on its own. In this platform, the workspace for DEV could be one stack, and the things inside it (clusters, `sp-sales-etl-dev`, grants) another.

A **stack dependency** is not code. It is a rule between two stacks: "run this one only after that one has applied."

**Why you need both:** the Databricks provider must connect to a real workspace. If the workspace and its contents share one stack, the plan fails, because the workspace doesn't exist yet. So you split them into two stacks. Then the stack dependency makes the contents stack wait for the workspace stack.

**Everyday comparison:** stacks are two separate jobs, like building a house and then furnishing it. The dependency is the rule that the movers only come after the builders finish.

**The lesson's example:** inside one stack, `databricks_metastore_assignment.this` refers to `azurerm_databricks_workspace.this.workspace_id`, so Terraform orders those two resources itself. A stack dependency does the same job one level up, between whole stacks.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that a stack dependency 'is not code' goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Deletes bronze and leaves the other two alone”?
check:0:0.a:
"Deletes bronze and leaves the other two alone" describes what you *meant*. It is not what Terraform does with `count`.

It gets one thing right. The bronze container does go away.

What it misses is how `count` names things. It names copies by position, not by what they are. Here is how the slots line up before and after you remove "bronze":

- `lake[0]`: was bronze, now silver. **Replace.**
- `lake[1]`: was silver, now gold. **Replace.**
- `lake[2]`: was gold, now nothing. **Delete.**

"Replace" means Terraform destroys the old container and creates a new, empty one. So the plan has two replaces and one delete.

Look at what that does to your data. The original silver and gold containers are destroyed. New silver and gold containers are created, but they start empty. In a team-sales data lake, that loses real data. If Spacelift showed you this plan and you approved the apply, the data would be gone.

"Replaces silver and gold, drops the last slot" is the better answer because it describes what Terraform actually plans: every later name shifts down one position, and the last slot is left with nothing.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing: the other two keep their names”?
check:0:2.a:
"Nothing" gets one thing right. You only meant to drop `bronze`, so you expect `silver` and `gold` to be left alone. That instinct is good.

It misses two things.

First, removing `bronze` is itself a change. The plan always deletes something, so "Nothing" can't be right under either approach.

Second, `count` doesn't know containers by their names. It knows them by position. Here is the list before and after:

- `[0]`: `bronze` becomes `silver`
- `[1]`: `silver` becomes `gold`
- `[2]`: `gold` becomes nothing

Terraform compares slot by slot. `[0]` and `[1]` now hold different names, so it plans to replace them. Replace means destroy the container and create a new, empty one. `[2]` has no item left, so it is deleted. In a Spacelift plan for `team-sales`, that means the data in all three containers is lost.

With `for_each`, each container is known by its key, like `["silver"]`. The plan would delete only `bronze` and leave `silver` and `gold` untouched.

"Replaces silver and gold, drops the last slot" is better because it follows how `count` matches by position, not by name.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The first 'miss' (removing bronze is itself a change) is weak, but it is not wrong.

check:1:1.q: Why not “It creates the containers faster”?
check:1:1.a:
"It creates the containers faster" sounds reasonable, but speed isn't the difference. Terraform builds independent resources at the same time either way. Ten containers made with `count` take about as long as ten made with `for_each`. So this option doesn't get anything right.

What it misses is the real risk: names. Terraform tracks each copy by an address, meaning the label it uses to remember which real container is which. With `count`, that label is a position, like `lake[0]` or `lake[1]`. Suppose team-sales asks to drop the first container from their YAML list. Every later container shifts down one position. Terraform sees new labels and plans to replace them. For storage containers, replace means delete and recreate, so the data is lost. In Spacelift, that would show up in the proposed plan as a string of destroys you never asked for.

With `for_each`, each container is labelled by a key, like `lake["silver"]`. Removing `bronze` leaves `silver` untouched.

"Each keeps its name when another is removed" is better because it names the actual reason: stable keys mean removing one container never forces Terraform to replace the others.

judge.notes: The claim that Terraform builds independent resources at the same time goes beyond the lesson, though it is true and does not contradict it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “It stops anyone deleting a container”?
check:1:2.a:
That option sounds close, but it promises too much.

**What it gets right:** with `for_each`, removing one container doesn't put the others at risk. Say the list is `bronze`, `silver`, `gold`, and you drop `bronze`. With `count`, `silver` moves from `[1]` to `[0]` and `gold` from `[2]` to `[1]`. Terraform sees new names and replaces both, which wipes their data. With `for_each`, `silver` and `gold` keep their names, so they stay untouched.

**What it misses:** `for_each` doesn't stop deletion. If someone removes `bronze` from the YAML in the config repo, the Spacelift plan will still say "delete `azurerm_storage_container.lake["bronze"]`", and an approved apply will delete it. Stopping deletions is a different job. Terraform's `prevent_destroy` setting can do it; that setting makes Terraform refuse any plan that would destroy the resource. A Spacelift policy check can also block it.

**Why the other answer is better:** "Each keeps its name when another is removed" names the real benefit. Containers are tracked by key, not position, so one removal never ripples into replacing the rest.

judge.notes: Minor only: the closing part runs to two sentences instead of one, and the prevent_destroy and Spacelift-policy remarks go beyond the lesson, though they are accurate and don't contradict it.

check:2:1.a:
That option pairs the right two names. Gold really was `lake[2]`, and it really should become `lake["gold"]`. But the direction is backwards.

A `moved` block reads like a change of address. `from` is the **old** name, the one Terraform's state file already knows. The state file is Terraform's record of what it built. `to` is the **new** name your code now uses.

Under `count`, the state file holds gold as `lake[2]`. Nothing called `lake["gold"]` exists there yet. So `from = lake["gold"]` points at nothing, and Terraform has nothing to move.

The plan in your Spacelift stack would then show two actions. It would delete `lake[2]`, because your `for_each` code no longer has that name. It would create a new, empty `lake["gold"]`. The gold container's data would be gone.

The right block:

```hcl
moved {
  from = azurerm_storage_container.lake[2]
  to   = azurerm_storage_container.lake["gold"]
}
```

"From `lake[2]` to `lake["gold"]`" is better because it starts from the name Terraform already has. Terraform renames gold in place, so the container and its data are kept.

check:2:2.a:
The `to` side is right. `lake["gold"]` is the new name gold should have under `for_each`. The block shape is right too: old address in `from`, new address in `to`. (An "address" is the name Terraform uses to track one real container.)

The problem is the `from` side. Under `count`, `lake[0]` was the first item in the list, which was bronze, not gold. A `moved` block tells Terraform "this real container now goes by a new name." So this block would hand the bronze container to the name `"gold"`. Bronze and its data would be filed under the wrong key.

Meanwhile the real gold container, `lake[2]`, gets no `moved` block. The `for_each` code no longer creates anything called `lake[2]`, so Terraform plans to destroy it, and its data goes with it. You would spot that in the Spacelift proposed plan as a destroy on the gold container.

The better answer, from `lake[2]` to `lake["gold"]`, points the old position that actually held gold at its new key, so gold keeps its container and its data.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Key repeated resources with for_each” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
It matters because a small YAML edit can wipe out real data.

Say team-sales has three storage containers in its lake, made with `count`. `bronze` sits at `[0]`, `silver` at `[1]` and `gold` at `[2]`. The team no longer needs `bronze`, so they delete that line from their YAML.

Now `silver` moves to `[0]` and `gold` moves to `[1]`. Terraform matches copies by position. It sees that `[0]` changed from bronze to silver and `[1]` changed from silver to gold. It also sees that `[2]` is gone. So its plan replaces `[0]` and `[1]` and deletes `[2]`. "Replace" means destroy the old container and create a new, empty one. Every file in silver and gold would be lost.

In Spacelift, the proposed plan would show several replacements, not one simple removal. If a reviewer skims the plan and approves it in PROD, that lake data is gone.

With `for_each`, each container is known by its key, like `["silver"]`. Removing `bronze` deletes only `["bronze"]`. The others keep their names, so Terraform leaves them alone.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare names position by position” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "Say `team-sales` asks for storage containers `bronze`, `silver` and `gold`, built with `count`. Terraform knows them only by position: `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`. If `bronze` is removed from the YAML, `silver` slides into slot `[0]`. Terraform sees a different container in that slot and plans a replace. A replace deletes the container, and its data goes with it."

**The idea:** "To predict the damage, I line up the old list and the new list. Then I compare them slot by slot. If a slot holds the same name, nothing changes. If the name differs, Terraform replaces it."

**The edge case:** "Removing the *last* item is safe. Nothing shifts, so only that one container goes. Removing the *first* item shifts every container after it."

**A likely follow-up**

*"How would you switch an existing `count` resource to `for_each` without losing data?"*

Hint: Mention `moved` blocks. Each one tells Terraform that the old slot, like `[1]`, is now the key `["silver"]`. Then check the Spacelift proposed plan in DEV. It should show no replacements before anyone approves the apply.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
The clearest warning sign shows up in the Spacelift proposed plan, before anything is applied. A plan is Terraform's preview of what it is about to do.

**What you would see**

- You remove one item from a YAML list, say the `bronze` container. You expect one delete.
- Instead, the plan lists several containers as "must be replaced". Replaced means destroy and then create again.
- The plan summary looks out of proportion, such as "2 to add, 3 to destroy" for a one-line edit.
- Resource addresses end in numbers, like `azurerm_storage_container.lake[1]`. An address is the name Terraform tracks a resource by.

**If it slips through**

- After the apply, the `silver` and `gold` containers exist but are empty.
- Databricks jobs for team-sales start failing with "path not found" errors on data that was there yesterday.
- It often passes in DEV, where data is throwaway, and only hurts in UAT or PROD.

**Quickest check**

Read the plan. Compare how many changes it lists against how many lines you changed. Then look at the addresses. Numbered addresses next to a removed item mean shifting. Named keys like `["silver"]` should stay steady.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The 2-add/3-destroy example matches removing the first of three count items, and the answer stays just under 200 words.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the rule needs extra care.

**1. The keys themselves change.** `for_each` is only safe while keys stay put. If `team-sales` is renamed to `team-sales-emea` in `env.yml`, its key changes, and Terraform replaces everything under it. Build keys from names that never change. When a rename is unavoidable, add a `moved` block in the same pull request.

**2. Keys aren't known until apply.** `for_each` keys must be known when the plan is made. Apply is the later step that actually builds things. So you can't key on something Terraform only learns during apply, like the ID of `sp-sales-etl-dev` created in the same run. Key on plain strings from the YAML instead.

**3. Moving between stacks.** A `moved` block only works inside one state file. A state file is Terraform's record of what it built, and each Spacelift stack has its own. Shifting a container from Foundation to Service needs a `removed` block in one stack and an `import` block in the other.

`count` still suits a simple on/off switch, like "create only in PROD."

learn:term.a:
Picture the sales team's data lake in DEV. `team-sales` lists three storage containers in its YAML: `bronze`, `silver` and `gold`. A storage container is a folder-like bucket in Azure that holds files. The Terraform code creates them with `count`, so they are known as `lake[0]`, `lake[1]` and `lake[2]`.

Later the team drops `bronze` from the YAML. Now `silver` sits at position 0 and `gold` at position 1.

Terraform compares by position. It sees that `lake[0]` used to be named `bronze` and is now `silver`. A container can't be renamed in place, so Terraform plans to replace it. Replace means delete it and create a new, empty one. The same happens to `lake[1]`. Then `lake[2]` is simply deleted.

So one small YAML edit plans to wipe out the `silver` and `gold` data. Spacelift shows this in the proposed plan. But a busy reviewer could approve it, and in PROD that is real data gone.

With `for_each`, each container is known by its key, like `lake["silver"]`. Removing `bronze` touches only `lake["bronze"]`. The others keep their names, so Terraform leaves them alone.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Adding or changing a tag”?

check:0:2.q: Why not “No change: a workspace is never replaced”?
check:0:2.a:
"No change: a workspace is never replaced" sounds safe, but it isn't true. That's what makes it risky.

**What it gets partly right:** many workspace changes do happen *in place*. That means Terraform edits the existing workspace without destroying it. Adding a tag is a good example. The plan marks these with `~`.

**What it misses:** some attributes can't be edited in place. Change one, and Terraform must destroy the workspace and build a new one. The plan marks that with `-/+`. On a Databricks workspace, that means a new URL. Everything inside is lost, such as clusters, notebooks and jobs for team-sales.

Believing a workspace is "never replaced" is the dangerous part. You might skim the proposed plan in Spacelift and approve the apply without looking for `-/+`. In PROD, that mistake would be costly.

**Why "Changing `managed_resource_group_name`" is better:** it names a real attribute that forces replacement. The `managed_resource_group_name` is the Azure resource group that Databricks creates and controls for the workspace. The lesson's plan shows it marked `-/+` with `# forces replacement`.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The workspace gets a new tag, nothing more”?
check:1:1.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Something in the workspace's settings did change, and often it is a small-looking edit, like one attribute in the Service stage's Terraform code.

But it misreads the mark. A simple tag change is an "update in place": Terraform edits the existing workspace and leaves it running. The plan marks that with `~`, like this:

```
~ resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "this" {
  ~ tags = { ... }
```

`-/+` means something different. Some attributes, like `managed_resource_group_name`, can't be edited on a live workspace. Changing them **forces replacement**: Terraform deletes the old workspace and creates a fresh one.

For team-sales, that means the workspace URL changes. The clusters, notebooks and other work inside it are gone. Access set up for groups like `grp-sales-dev-owners` must be rebuilt. A tag change is harmless. This is not.

So when Spacelift shows a proposed plan, look at the mark, not the size of the edit.

"A new workspace, with a new URL and nothing in it" is better because it describes what `-/+` really does: destroy the old workspace and build an empty new one.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The workspace restarts and keeps its contents”?
check:1:2.a:
"The workspace restarts and keeps its contents" sounds safe, but that is not what `-/+` means.

**What it gets right:** something big does happen to the workspace. And afterwards there is still a workspace with the same name in your Terraform code, so it can look like the "same" one came back.

**What it misses:** `-/+` is the plan's mark for a replacement. Terraform first **destroys** the old workspace, then **creates** a brand new one. Nothing is carried over. check:2:0.q: Why not “Approve: ten is a fair sample”?

The problem is what "sample" means here. A sample is a small part you check to guess about the whole. That works when one miss is cheap. Here, one miss is not cheap.

A `-/+` (the plan's mark for a replacement) means Terraform destroys a resource and creates a new one. Picture a Service stage plan in Spacelift for PROD. If change 27 is the team-sales workspace with `managed_resource_group_name` changing, that workspace gets a new URL and loses everything inside it. Checking ten changes tells you nothing about the other thirty. A `-/+` could be change 11 or change 40.

So the risk isn't spread evenly, like a coin toss. One hidden replacement is enough to cause real damage, and only a full check rules it out.

"Check the other thirty for `-/+` too" is better because you approve only after every change has been looked at, so no replacement can slip through.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Ask for the plan to be split up”?

"Ask for the plan to be split up" gets one thing right. It notices that 40 changes is a lot to check, and that only ten have been looked at.

But splitting doesn't answer the question in front of you. The same 40 changes would still be there, just in smaller pieces. Any `-/+` hiding in the unchecked thirty would still be hiding. If one of those thirty is the `azurerm_databricks_workspace`, approving the apply would give the workspace a new URL and lose everything inside it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Keep changes with delete and create” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The problem.** In our Service stage, one small YAML edit can change an attribute like `managed_resource_group_name`. Terraform can't change that "in place" (editing the existing thing). So it destroys the workspace and builds a new one. That means a new URL, and everything inside the workspace is lost.

**The idea.** Terraform can save its plan as JSON (a structured text format code can read). In it, each resource change has a list called `actions`. A replacement is the case where that list holds both `"delete"` and `"create"`. So I collect only those resource addresses, in plan order. Then reviewers see them before anyone approves the apply in Spacelift.

**Edge case.** The two words don't always come in the same order. With the setting `create_before_destroy`, Terraform builds the new resource first, so `actions` is `["create", "delete"]`. Check that both are present, not their order. And a plain `"delete"` is risky too, but it deserves its own separate warning.

**Likely follow-up:** "Where would this check live?"
*Hint:* Make it a Spacelift policy on the proposed plan. A policy is an automatic rule the plan must pass. That way, a PROD workspace replacement gets blocked or needs extra sign-off before apply.

judge.notes: No major problems. The create_before_destroy order point goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs a replacement slipped through**

The worst sign comes after apply. A workspace in DEV, UAT or PROD has a **new URL**. Product teams like `team-sales` report that their notebooks, jobs and clusters are gone. Bookmarks and links stop working.

Earlier hints show up in the Spacelift proposed plan (the dry run you review before approving):

- The summary line has destroy counts that don't fit the change. Say a small YAML edit, like renaming `managed_resource_group_name`, gives "1 to add, 1 to destroy" when you expected only "1 to change". The summary only gives counts. It won't tell you which resource is affected, but the mismatch is your cue to look closer.
- A resource you expected to update in place (marked `~`) instead shows `-/+`.

**Quickest check**

Open the text plan in the proposed run. Search for `-/+` and for `# forces replacement`. Each `-/+` gives the resource address, such as `azurerm_databricks_workspace.this`. The `# forces replacement` comment marks the attribute causing it. If a workspace shows up there, stop before approving.

learn:stops.a:
**When does this stop working?**

**1. A plain delete is just as dangerous.**
Say someone removes `team-sales` from `env.yml`. The plan may show only `"delete"` for that team's catalog, with no `"create"`. It is not a replacement, so a check for replacements skips it. Also flag plain deletes on important resources, and add a Spacelift policy that blocks them in UAT and PROD.

**2. A renamed key looks like two separate changes.**
Imagine a `for_each` key changes from `sales` to `team-sales`. (`for_each` makes one resource per item in a map.) Terraform sees one address deleted and a different address created. Each change has only one action, so neither looks like a replacement, but the old one is still destroyed. Use a `moved` block to tell Terraform it is the same resource under a new name.

**3. The text mark can differ.**
With `create_before_destroy`, Terraform builds the new resource first. The text plan then shows `+/-` instead of `-/+`. Read the `actions` list in the JSON plan, not the symbols. For the workspace itself, also set `prevent_destroy` as a safety net. It makes Terraform refuse any plan that would destroy it.

judge.notes: No check fails. Each point runs to 4-5 sentences against the 2-3 asked for, and the total is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:term.a:
**"Forces replacement"** means Terraform can't edit the resource where it stands. It has to destroy it and build a brand-new one.

**Everyday comparison:** you can repaint a house while living in it. You can't move its foundation that way. To change the foundation, you knock the house down and build again. Everything inside goes with the old house.

Terraform works the same way. Some attributes (settings on a resource) can change in place, like a tag. Others are fixed once the resource exists. Change one of those, and Terraform plans a delete followed by a create.

In the lesson's example, the plan shows:

```
-/+ resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "this" {
  ~ managed_resource_group_name = "a" -> "b" # forces replacement
```

- `-/+` marks a replacement: delete (`-`), then create (`+`).
- `~` marks the attribute that changed, from `"a"` to `"b"`.
- `# forces replacement` names the attribute causing it.

For a team like team-sales, this means a new workspace URL and losing the clusters, notebooks and jobs inside. So in the Spacelift proposed plan, find every `-/+` before approving.

check:0:0.a:
"Adopt it automatically" sounds sensible. The storage account really does exist in Azure, and your resource block uses the same name, `stsalesdev`. A human would spot the match.

Terraform doesn't work that way. It plans from its **state**, which is its own saved list of the things it manages. It does not search Azure for something with a matching name. If an address like `azurerm_storage_account.landing` is not in state, Terraform assumes the resource doesn't exist yet.

So the plan proposes a new storage account. In a Spacelift stack, that proposed plan could even pass review. The apply then fails, because Azure says the name `stsalesdev` is already taken.

Adopting only happens when you ask for it. You add an `import` block with the resource's address and its Azure ID. Then the plan says "1 to import". Even then, read the rest of that plan in case your code doesn't match the real resource.

"Create a new one with the same name" is right because it describes what Terraform does when the resource is missing from state: it plans a create, unaware that the name is already in use.

judge.notes: No real problems; the Spacelift 'could pass review' remark goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:2.a:
"Nothing" is a very human guess. The storage account really does exist in Azure. Your resource block even describes it. So it feels like there is nothing left to do.

The catch is where Terraform looks. It does not scan Azure to see what is already there. It plans from its **state**, which is its own record of the things it manages. Nobody ever added `stsalesdev` to that record, because someone made it by hand in the portal.

So Terraform compares your code to its state. It finds `azurerm_storage_account.landing` in the code and no matching entry in the state. To Terraform, that means "this is new", and the plan says "1 to add".

In a Spacelift run for the DEV stack, the proposed plan would look harmless. Then the approved apply would fail, because Azure says the name `stsalesdev` is already taken.

"Create a new one with the same name" is better because it describes what Terraform actually plans when the resource is missing from state and there is no `import` block.

check:1:0.a:
"1 to add" gets one thing right. The storage account isn't in Terraform's **state** (its record of what it manages). So Terraform doesn't know it exists. Without an import block, the plan would indeed say "1 to add".

But you added an import block, and that changes the plan. "Add" means Terraform will **create** a brand-new storage account. It would try to make another `stsalesdev` in `rg-sales-dev`. The name is already taken, so the apply would fail. In Spacelift, the proposed plan would look fine, then the approved apply would break.

The import block tells Terraform something different. It says: "this resource already exists at this Azure ID, so link it to the address `azurerm_storage_account.landing` and start tracking it." Nothing new gets built. Terraform just writes the real resource into its state.

So the summary should say "1 to import". Also check that the same plan shows no changes or replacements for that resource. That tells you your code matches what's really there.

"1 to import" is better because it means Terraform adopts the storage account that already exists instead of trying to build a second one.

judge.notes: The claim that the Spacelift proposed plan would 'look fine' is not in the lesson, but it fits the lesson's point that the apply is what fails. Length is close to the 200-word limit.

check:1:2.a:
"1 to destroy" is not what this plan should say.

**Destroy** means Terraform plans to delete a real resource. It only plans that for something already in its **state** (its record of what it manages) that your code no longer describes. The hand-made `stsalesdev` account isn't in state yet. So Terraform has nothing on its list to destroy.

There is a small grain of truth here. If your `azurerm_storage_account.landing` block doesn't match the real account, some differences force a **replace**. That means delete and recreate. The plan would then show a destroy alongside the import. But that is a warning sign, not the goal. In a Spacelift proposed run, you'd fix the code before anyone approves the apply.

What the import block actually does is adopt the account. Terraform reads it from Azure and writes it into state. Nothing is made, changed or deleted.

"1 to import" is better because it describes exactly that: the existing account joins Terraform's state untouched, and that is the clean result you're aiming for.

judge.notes: No real problems. The line 'Nothing is made, changed or deleted' only holds when the code already matches the real account, but the answer covers the mismatch case just before.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Apply it: changes are harmless”?
check:2:0.a:
It's true that the import part is safe. Adopting `stsalesdev` only records it in Terraform's **state**, the file where Terraform tracks what it manages. Nothing in Azure changes from that alone.

The problem is the other lines in the same plan. Those changes aren't part of adopting. They mean your resource block doesn't match the real account. Applying would rewrite the live account to match your code, including any settings you guessed or left out.

That is not harmless. Say team-sales relies on a network rule or access setting that your block doesn't include. Applying would change it on the real account, and their jobs could stop working. Some differences are worse: the plan may say **replace**, which means delete the account and make a new one. The data in `stsalesdev` would be lost.

You also can't tell these risks apart by guessing. Each changed line needs checking against what actually exists.

"Fix the code to match it first" is better because it keeps going until the plan shows only "1 to import" and nothing to change, so Terraform truly just adopts the account.

check:2:1.a:
Removing the `import` block gets one thing right. You noticed the plan would change a real account, and you stopped it. Pausing there is good instinct.

But it doesn't solve the problem. It only swaps it for a different one.

Your `resource "azurerm_storage_account" "landing"` block is still in the code. Without the `import` block, Terraform has no record of `stsalesdev` in its **state** (its own list of what it manages). So the next Spacelift proposed plan says "1 to add". Terraform tries to create the account again. The apply fails because the name `stsalesdev` is already taken.

If you delete the resource block too, you're back where you started. The account stays hand-made and unmanaged.

The real issue is the mismatch. Your code describes settings that differ from the live account. Removing the import hides that mismatch for now. It doesn't fix it.

"Fix the code to match it first" is better. It keeps the import and corrects the code, so the plan shows only "1 to import" with no changes. Then you adopt the account exactly as it is.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the closing explanation runs to two sentences rather than the requested one, which is minor.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Adopt existing resources with an import block” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Terraform only knows about what is in its **state**, its saved record of what it manages. Anything built by hand is invisible to it.

So if your code describes something that already exists, the plan says "create". The apply then fails with an error like: "A resource with the ID ... already exists - to be managed via Terraform this resource needs to be imported into the State". That means someone made it by hand, often the network team.

Example: the network team made the subnet `snet-sales-dev` in the portal for the team-sales workspace. Your Service stage also declares it. The Spacelift apply in DEV fails, and the stack is stuck.

The tempting fix is to delete the subnet so Terraform can recreate it. Don't. The workspace may already use it, so running clusters could lose their network. The network team's settings would be lost too.

Instead, add an `import` block with the resource's address (its name in your code, like `azurerm_subnet.sales_dev`) and its Azure ID. The plan shows "1 to import". Then read the rest of the plan. If it would change anything, fix your code to match the real subnet.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “In state, imported, or new” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* Terraform plans from its state. That is the record of what it manages. Say someone made `stsalesdev` by hand in the Azure portal. It isn't in state, so Terraform thinks it doesn't exist and plans to create it. The apply then fails because the name is taken.

*The idea.* So every resource address in the code falls into one of three groups. An address is a name like `azurerm_storage_account.landing`. Already in state means nothing to do. Not in state but with an `import` block means Terraform adopts the existing resource, and the plan says "1 to import". Anything else is a real add.

*The trade-off.* Import is not a free pass. If the code doesn't match the real resource, the same plan also changes it, or even replaces it. So I read the whole plan and adjust the code until the import changes nothing.

**A likely follow-up**

"In Spacelift, how would you catch a risky import before it reaches PROD?"

Hint: mention reviewing the proposed plan in DEV. Then add a policy check that blocks any import that also updates or replaces the resource.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
## Warning signs

**The plan wants to add something that already exists.** In Spacelift's proposed plan, `azurerm_storage_account.landing` shows as "1 to add", but `stsalesdev` is already in the portal. Then the approved apply fails. The azurerm provider says a resource with that ID already exists and needs to be imported.

**A quiet duplicate appears.** If the name in your code differs slightly from the real one, nothing fails. Terraform simply builds a second storage account next to the hand-made one. That's the second sofa. Watch for near-twin names in `rg-sales-dev`.

**The import comes with surprises.** The summary says "1 to import" but also "1 to change", or even "1 to destroy". Changes are marked `~`. A replace is marked `-/+` with "forces replacement". A replace means the real account gets deleted and rebuilt, and the data in it is lost.

## Quickest check

Before approving, read the plan's summary line. A clean adoption reads "1 to import, 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy". Anything else means your code and the real resource still disagree.

judge.notes: No real problems. The error wording, the `-/+` marker and the data-loss warning go beyond the lesson, but they are accurate and do not contradict it.

learn:stops.a:
The rule holds, but these three situations need extra care.

**Someone keeps editing it by hand.** Say a person still tweaks the `stsalesdev` storage account in the Azure portal. After import, every plan will undo their edits to match the code. Agree first that all changes go through the YAML config repo, then import.

**Another stack already manages it.** If the Foundation stack already has a resource in its state (its saved list of what it manages), importing it into a Service stack gives it two owners. Each apply could overwrite the other's settings. Pick exactly one stack to own each resource. Take it out of the old owner before importing it into the new one.

**There are dozens of hand-made resources.** Picture every cluster and service principal that team-sales built by hand in DEV. Matching all that code in one go is slow and easy to get wrong. Work in small batches. Make each Spacelift plan show "import" and no changes before moving on. Then repeat through UAT and PROD.

learn:term.a:
**State** is Terraform's own record of what it manages. Think of a stock list kept by a storeroom clerk. The clerk trusts only the list. If someone carried a box in and never wrote it down, the clerk says "we don't have that" and orders another.

Terraform works the same way. Its state is a file that pairs each **resource address** (the name in your code, like `azurerm_storage_account.landing`) with the real Azure ID it points to. Every plan compares your code with that state.

In the lesson's example, someone made `stsalesdev` by hand in the Azure portal. It really exists in `rg-sales-dev`, but it isn't in state. So when Spacelift runs the plan, Terraform thinks it must create it. The apply then fails because the name is taken.

The `import` block fixes this. It tells Terraform to write the existing resource into its state:

- `to` is the address in your code.
- `id` is the Azure ID of the real resource.

After the apply, `stsalesdev` is on the list. Later plans treat it as already managed.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Whenever a run is blocked by it”?
check:0:0.a:
"Whenever a run is blocked by it" gets one thing right. A blocked run is often the first sign of a problem. A crashed run can leave its lock behind, a "stale" lock that nobody will ever release. In that case, `terraform force-unlock` is exactly the fix.

What it misses: being blocked doesn't tell you *why*. The same error appears when the holder is still alive and working. Look at the example. `Who: spacelift@worker-7` and `Operation: OperationTypeApply` could mean a Spacelift apply on the `dbx-service-dev` stack is changing the DEV workspace right now. If you force-unlock then, your run and that apply both write the state file. That is the corruption the lock exists to prevent.

So the block is your cue to investigate, not your permission to unlock. Read `Who` and `Created`, then check that stack's runs in Spacelift to see whether that apply is still going or has died.

"Once the run holding it has stopped" is better because it ties the unlock to the one fact that makes it safe: nobody else can still be writing the state.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Never: a lock clears on its own”?
check:0:2.a:
"Never: a lock clears on its own" gets one thing right. You shouldn't rush to `terraform force-unlock`. If the run holding the lock is still working, it will release the lock when it finishes. Breaking it early lets two runs write the state at once, and that is how state gets corrupted.

What it misses is the crashed run. A lock is only released by the run that took it. If that run dies partway through, nothing comes back to clean up. Picture the `spacelift@worker-7` apply on `dbx-service-dev` crashing. The azurerm backend keeps the lock on the state file, which Azure calls a blob. Here it is `tfstate/dbx-service-dev.tfstate`. The lock stays until someone removes it. Every later plan or apply on that stack fails with the same error. Waiting forever won't fix it.

So the real question isn't whether to force-unlock. It's when. First read the lock info to see who holds it. Then confirm that run is truly dead.

"Once the run holding it has stopped" is better because it allows the one safe case for force-unlocking: a stuck lock with no live writer left to collide with.

judge.notes: No real problems. The only point to watch is the claim that a lock is only released by the run that took it. The lesson does not state this, though it does not contradict it.

check:1:1.a:
"Run `terraform force-unlock` now" gets one thing right. `terraform force-unlock` is the real command for clearing a lock, and it would make the error go away.

But it skips the check the lesson asks for: is the run holding the lock really dead? Here it isn't. The lock info says another run took the lock two minutes ago, and that run is still planning. Think of a Spacelift run on the `dbx-service-dev` stack that is busy comparing your YAML-driven config with what exists in Azure Databricks.

The lock exists so only one run touches the state at a time. State is Terraform's record of what it manages. If you remove the lock while that run is alive, your run and its run could both write the state blob. That's the stored state file in the Azure storage account. Two writers at once can corrupt it. Then Terraform's record no longer matches what really exists.

`terraform force-unlock` is for a lock left behind by a crashed run, not a busy one.

"Wait for that run to finish" is better because the lock is doing its job, and it will be released on its own when that healthy run completes.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Delete the state file and retry”?
check:1:2.a:
It's a tempting shortcut. Deleting the state file would make the lock error go away, because the lock sits on that file. That's about all it gets right.

What it misses is that **state** is Terraform's only record of what it manages. In this stack it's the blob `tfstate/dbx-service-dev.tfstate` in the Azure storage account. That file is how Terraform knows it already created team-sales's clusters, the `sp-sales-etl-dev` service principal, and the access for `grp-sales-dev-owners`.

Delete it, and Terraform forgets all of that. The next plan would try to create everything again. You'd get errors about things that already exist, or duplicates you'd have to clean up by hand.

It also ignores what the lock info told you. The other run took the lock two minutes ago and is still planning. Nothing is broken. The lock is doing its job by stopping two runs from writing state at once.

"Wait for that run to finish" is better because the lock holder is alive and will release the lock on its own, so waiting keeps state safe and costs only a few minutes.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Both applies just run more slowly”?
check:2:0.a:
"Both applies just run more slowly" treats this as a speed problem. Speed isn't what's at risk here.

**State** is Terraform's record of what it manages. For example, it tracks which clusters and service principals exist for `team-sales` in DEV. Each apply reads that record, changes things in Azure Databricks, then writes the record back.

With no lock, two applies on the same stack can write that record at the same moment. One write can overwrite or garble the other. The record may end up broken, or no longer match what really exists. Terraform could then try to create `sp-sales-etl-dev` again, or lose track of a cluster.

That is why runs take a **lock** first. A lock is a "busy" marker on the state. With one in place, the second run doesn't quietly slow down. It stops with `Error acquiring the state lock`, as in the lesson's example.

"The state record could get corrupted" is better because it names the real danger: two runs writing the same record at once, which is exactly what the lock prevents.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Terraform keeps the newer code”?
check:2:1.a:
"Terraform keeps the newer code" sounds safe, but Terraform has no such rule.

**What it gets right:** it senses that two runs clash, and that one run's changes might win over the other's.

**What it misses:** Terraform never compares the two runs and picks a winner. It doesn't look at whose code is newer at all. Each apply just changes real resources and then writes its results into the state file. State is Terraform's record of what it manages.

Picture two teammates applying the `dbx-service-dev` stack at the same moment. One adds a cluster for `team-sales`. The other adds `sp-sales-etl-dev`. Both runs write to `dbx-service-dev.tfstate` at once. Their writes can overlap or overwrite each other. The record might end up missing the cluster, even though it really exists in the workspace. Or the file might end up half-written and unreadable.

So the danger isn't about which code wins. It's that the record itself breaks. That is why runs take a lock first.

**Why "The state record could get corrupted" is better:** it names the real risk, which is that the record stops matching what actually exists in Azure.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Start reading at the heading” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** A lock error from the `dbx-service-dev` stack has lines above the lock details. One is `Error message: state blob is already locked`. That line has a colon too. If I split every line at its colon, that noise gets mixed in with the real lock fields.

**The idea.** So I only start reading at the `Lock Info:` heading. A yes-or-no flag called `inside` starts at no. It flips to yes when I reach the heading. Only the lines after that get cut into a key and a value.

**An edge case.** If the heading never appears, I get an empty result. That's the honest answer: there's no lock info, so I shouldn't guess. I also cut each line at the first colon only, so the `Created` time keeps its own colons.

**A follow-up an interviewer might ask**

"The lock says `Who: spacelift@worker-7`. Do you force-unlock right away?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Not yet. Open that stack's runs in Spacelift and check whether the apply is still going. Only once you're sure that run is dead, run `terraform force-unlock` with that exact lock `ID`. The `ID` is the unique label Terraform gave this lock.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that someone force-unlocked without checking**

- The next plan for `dbx-service-dev` wants to create things that already exist, like a cluster for `team-sales`. That means the state, Terraform's record of what it manages, lost track of them.
- An apply fails with "already exists" errors, or `sp-sales-etl-dev` shows up twice in the workspace.
- Spacelift shows two applies on the same stack that overlapped in time.
- The state blob's history in the Azure storage account shows two writes seconds apart.

**Warning signs that the lock error was read wrong**

- The `Created` time looks cut short, like `2026-10-09 23`, with the minutes and seconds gone.
- Keys or values have stray spaces, so a lookup for `Who` finds nothing.

**Quickest check**

Read `Who` and `Created` first. Here `Who` is `spacelift@worker-7`, so a Spacelift run took the lock. Open that stack's runs in Spacelift. If an apply started near `23:25:51 UTC` is still running, the lock is real. Wait for it to finish. Only consider `terraform force-unlock` once you've confirmed that run is truly dead.

Here are three situations where the rule or the method needs extra care.

**1. The lock holder is still running.**
Say `Who` shows `spacelift@worker-7` and that apply on `dbx-service-dev` is still going. Then the lock is doing its job. Don't run `terraform force-unlock`. Force-unlocking means removing the lock by hand, and two runs writing state at once would corrupt it. Only unlock once you've confirmed that run is really dead.

**2. Spacelift manages the stack's state.**
This lesson's stack keeps state in an Azure storage account (the `azurerm` backend). A stack whose state Spacelift manages never shows this error. So for that kind of stack, there's no lock message to read. Look at the stack's runs instead.

**3. The error has no `Lock Info:` heading.**
The `inside` flag only turns to yes at that heading. If the heading is missing, nothing gets stored, and you end up with an empty lookup table. An empty table tells you nothing about who holds the lock. Treat it as "unknown", not as "safe to unlock", and check the stack's runs by hand.

learn:term.a:
Think of a shared stock ledger in a warehouse. It lists every item the warehouse owns and where it sits. Before anyone orders or removes stock, they check the ledger first.

Terraform's **state** is that ledger. It is a file listing everything Terraform has built for you. In this platform, that means workspaces, clusters from `clusters.yml`, and service principals like `sp-sales-etl-dev`. On each run, Terraform compares three things: your code, the state, and what really exists in Azure. The differences become the plan.

If two runs wrote the ledger at the same moment, entries could get scrambled. So a run takes a **lock** first, like signing the ledger out.

In the lesson's example, look at this line:

```
  Path:      tfstate/dbx-service-dev.tfstate
```

That is the state file for the Service stage in DEV. It lives as a blob in an Azure storage account. A blob is just a file stored in Azure. The `Who` and `Operation` lines show that a Spacelift worker signed it out to run an apply.

check:0:0.q: Why not “1 to add, 1 to destroy: a new cluster”?
check:0:0.a:
"1 to add, 1 to destroy" is a real plan. It's just the plan for a different situation: the rename *without* a `moved` block.

Here's what it gets right. Terraform does match its **state** (its saved record of what exists) to your code by **address**, the resource's name in code. So if you change `databricks_cluster.etl` to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl` and do nothing else, the old address looks gone and the new one looks brand new. The proposed plan in the team-sales Spacelift stack would then destroy the cluster and create a fresh one.

What it misses is the `moved` block. That block links the two addresses. Terraform walks through the old addresses and finds `databricks_cluster.etl` gone from the code. Instead of marking it for destroy, it sees that a move points it at `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. It updates the name in state. Nothing is added and nothing is destroyed. The same cluster keeps running under its new name.

"The cluster moves to its new address" is better because the `moved` block turns a destroy-and-create into a simple rename in state, so the real cluster is never touched.

check:0:2.q: Why not “An error: addresses can't change”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Terraform does care a lot about addresses. An **address** is the name Terraform uses to track a resource, like `databricks_cluster.etl`. Terraform matches what is in its **state** (its saved record of what exists) to your code by that address.

But changing an address is allowed. It is not an error. Without a moved block, Terraform treats the rename as two separate things. The old address is gone, so it plans to destroy the cluster. The new address is unknown, so it plans to create one. That is risky for team-sales, because their running cluster would be torn down. Still, Terraform doesn't stop you.

The `moved` block exists to fix exactly this. It links the old name to the new one. So when Spacelift runs the proposed plan for the Service stack in DEV, Terraform updates the name in state. The plan shows nothing destroyed and nothing created.

"The cluster moves to its new address" is better because it describes what the `moved` block actually does: it updates the name in state, so the same cluster keeps running untouched.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A second copy of the cluster”?
check:1:1.a:
"A second copy of the cluster" has the right instinct: you don't want the real cluster destroyed. Keeping the old block `databricks_cluster.etl` next to the new `databricks_cluster.sales_etl` does stop the destroy.

But it fixes the wrong thing. Terraform still sees two separate addresses (the names it uses to track each resource). So the plan becomes "keep the old one, create a new one." You get two real clusters in the workspace. That means double the cost, and two clusters that team-sales and `sp-sales-etl-dev` might both be pointed at. The new cluster is also a fresh, empty one. It has a new cluster ID and none of the history of the one you meant to keep.

It also only delays the problem. When you later delete the old block to tidy up, the next Spacelift plan will destroy the old cluster after all.

A moved block is better because it tells Terraform the old address and the new address are the same cluster. Terraform then just updates the name in its state (its record of what exists), and nothing is destroyed or created.

judge.notes: The answer holds up against the lesson. The cluster ID and history point goes beyond the lesson but does not contradict it, and the final 'one sentence' on the moved block runs to two short sentences.

check:1:2.q: Why not “An import block for the old one”?
check:1:2.a:
An import block feels close, because it is also about keeping a real cluster instead of building a new one. That part of the instinct is right.

But import solves a different problem. An **import block** tells Terraform to start tracking a real cluster that its state (its record of what it manages) doesn't know about yet. Here, Terraform already knows the cluster. It just knows it under the old address, `databricks_cluster.etl`.

So importing doesn't fix the mismatch. The old address is still in state with no code behind it, and the plan would still destroy it. That destroys the very cluster you meant to keep. If you instead imported the cluster to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`, the same cluster would sit at two addresses, and the old one would still be marked for destroy.

Import also needs the cluster's real ID. That ID differs in DEV, UAT and PROD, so you'd need a separate value for each environment.

A moved block is better because it simply renames the existing entry in state from old to new, so nothing is destroyed, and the same block works in every environment.

judge.notes: The import-block details (needs a real ID, differs per environment) go beyond the lesson, but they are accurate and do not contradict it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “None: the rename is finished”?
check:2:0.a:
"None: the rename is finished" gets one thing right. In DEV, the rename really is done. DEV's state (Terraform's saved record of what it built) now knows the cluster as `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. Deleting the `moved` block changes nothing there.

What it misses is that each environment keeps its own state. DEV, UAT and PROD each run as a separate Spacelift stack. Applying in DEV does not touch PROD's record. PROD's state still lists the cluster under the old address, `databricks_cluster.etl`.

Now picture PROD's next plan without the `moved` block. Terraform walks through PROD's old addresses. `databricks_cluster.etl` is not in the code, and no move points it anywhere, so it gets marked for destroy. Then `databricks_cluster.sales_etl` is a new address with no link to anything old, so it gets marked for create. team-sales would lose its running PROD cluster and get a fresh one with a new ID.

"Prod destroys and recreates it" is better because it sees that the rename is only finished in environments that have already applied it, and PROD still needs the `moved` block to link the two names.

judge.notes: No real problems. Two small additions go beyond the lesson: that each environment is a separate Spacelift stack, and the 'new ID' detail. Both fit the lesson's setting and do not contradict it.

check:2:2.a:
"Dev loses the cluster" gets one thing right: deleting the `moved` block too early can cost you a cluster. It just points at the wrong environment.

Each environment has its own **state**. That is Terraform's record of what it built and the address it filed each thing under. Dev has already applied the rename. So Dev's state already lists the cluster as `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. That matches the code. With or without the `moved` block, Dev's plan shows no changes. Dev is safe.

Prod is the problem. Prod's state still lists the cluster as `databricks_cluster.etl`. Without the `moved` block, nothing links the old name to the new one. So Prod's Spacelift stack would propose a plan that sees `etl` gone from the code and `sales_etl` as brand new. That means destroy the old cluster, then create a fresh one. Any jobs running on it in PROD would be interrupted.

"Prod destroys and recreates it" is better because it names the environment that still needs the `moved` block, and it says exactly what the plan would do there.

judge.notes: The only extra claim is that jobs on the cluster would be interrupted. The lesson does not say this, but it follows from a destroy and does not contradict the lesson.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Rename with moved, not destroy and create” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
Terraform tracks each thing it built by its **address**, like `databricks_cluster.etl`. It keeps a record called **state** that links each address to the real object in Azure Databricks. Change the address in code, and Terraform thinks the old object should go and a new one should be made.

Here is what that costs. Say team-sales renames `databricks_cluster.etl` to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. The Spacelift plan for the Service stack now says: destroy one cluster, create one cluster. If someone approves it without reading closely, the running cluster is deleted. Jobs pointing at its cluster ID break. Access for `grp-sales-dev-owners` is gone until the new cluster gets it.

Identities are worse. Recreate the service principal `sp-sales-etl-dev` and it gets a new ID. Every permission tied to the old ID is lost.

A `moved` block avoids this. It tells Terraform the two addresses are the same object. The plan then shows a rename, with nothing destroyed. Keep the block in the code. UAT and PROD may not have applied the rename yet, and they need it too.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Keep, move, destroy, create” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**30-second answer**

*Problem:* Terraform knows each resource by its address, like `databricks_cluster.etl`. If I rename it to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`, the plan (Terraform's preview of changes) sees one address gone and a new one appear. So it would destroy team-sales's ETL cluster and build a fresh one.

*Idea:* A `moved` block links the old name to the new one. Terraform then sorts every address. Still in the code: keep. Gone, but a move points it to an address that exists: move. Gone with no move: destroy. Any brand-new address that no move points to: create. It's like a change-of-address card. Your post follows you.

*Edge case:* Leave the `moved` block in the code after the rename. DEV may have applied it already. But if PROD's Spacelift stack hasn't run yet, deleting the block makes PROD destroy and recreate.

**Likely follow-up:** "How would you prove a rename is safe before apply?"

*Hint:* Read the proposed plan in Spacelift. It should show the cluster as moved, with zero destroys. You could add a policy check that blocks any plan that destroys a cluster.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

The clearest sign is in the Spacelift proposed plan (the preview Terraform shows before anything changes). You only renamed `databricks_cluster.etl` to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. Yet the summary says something like "1 to add, 1 to destroy." A pure rename should never add or destroy anything.

If that plan gets approved anyway, the damage shows up after apply:

- The cluster has a new cluster ID, which is the unique number Databricks gives it.
- Jobs that pointed at the old ID fail with "cluster not found."
- Permissions granted outside Terraform, or libraries added by hand, are gone.
- Running jobs stop partway when the old cluster is deleted.

**A later trap**

DEV applied the rename fine. Then someone deleted the `moved` block before UAT or PROD ran. Those stages never saw the rename, so their plans suddenly show destroy plus create.

**Quickest check**

Read the plan before approving. A correct rename shows the resource "has moved to" the new address. The summary should read "0 to add, 0 to destroy." Anything else means the two names aren't linked.

judge.notes: No real problems. The cluster ID, job failure and lost-permission details go beyond the lesson but are plausible and don't contradict it. 'Anything else means the two names aren't linked' slightly overgeneralises.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Moving between stacks.** A `moved` block only works inside one state file. State is Terraform's record of what it built. Say a cluster moves from the Foundation stack to a Service stack in Spacelift. Those are two separate states, so `moved` can't link them. Instead, use a `removed` block in the old stack so it forgets the cluster without deleting it. Then use an `import` block in the new stack to adopt the cluster.

**2. Keys that come from YAML.** With `for_each`, addresses often use names read from team.yml, like `databricks_cluster.etl["team-sales"]`. If a team is renamed in the config repo, every key changes at once. You need one `moved` block per changed key, or each one becomes a destroy plus a create.

**3. Renames mixed with real changes.** A `moved` block fixes the name only. Say the same pull request also changes a setting the provider can't update in place. Then the plan still shows a replace, meaning destroy and recreate. Rename in one change, apply it through DEV, UAT and PROD, and only then change the settings.

judge.notes: No real problem. Minor: a cluster moving out of Foundation (account-level) is a slightly odd example, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:term.a:
An **address** is the name Terraform uses to find one resource. Think of a label on a drawer in a filing cabinet. Terraform keeps notes about each real thing it built in a file called **state**. Each note sits in a drawer, and the address is the label on that drawer.

An address has two parts joined by a dot. In `databricks_cluster.etl`, the first part, `databricks_cluster`, is the resource type: what kind of thing it is. The second part, `etl`, is the name you chose in the code.

Terraform matches code to state by these labels. Say you change the code to `databricks_cluster.sales_etl`. Terraform looks for a drawer with that label and finds none. It also sees the drawer `databricks_cluster.etl`, which no code points at anymore. So it plans to destroy the old cluster and create a new one.

That's why the lesson's example names both addresses:

```
moved {
  from = databricks_cluster.etl
  to   = databricks_cluster.sales_etl
}
```

This tells Terraform to relabel the drawer, not empty it. The real cluster in the team-sales workspace stays as it is.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Run init again every day”?
check:2:0.a:
"Run init again every day" is not the best answer. It does touch the right command. `terraform init` is the step that picks a provider version, the plugin Terraform uses to talk to Azure or Databricks. So the idea points in a sensible direction.

What it misses is the actual problem. The plans differ because your laptop and Spacelift ended up with different provider versions. Running init daily does not make them agree. Each place still runs init on its own and makes its own pick. New provider versions come out often, so the laptop and the Spacelift stack for team-sales in DEV could still land on different ones. A schedule does not tie them to one shared version, and nobody reviews the change.

The right answer is "Commit .terraform.lock.hcl." That file records the exact version init picked. Once it is in the repo, every run uses that same version until someone runs `terraform init -upgrade` and the change is reviewed.

Committing `.terraform.lock.hcl` is better because it gives every run, on any laptop or Spacelift stack, the same exact provider version until a reviewed upgrade changes it.

check:2:1.a:
Deleting the `.terraform` folder points at the right place, but it doesn't solve the problem.

**What it gets right:** `.terraform` is the local folder where `terraform init` stores the provider plugins it downloaded. So it does hold the version your laptop is using. Clearing it makes your laptop download again.

**What it misses:** without a lock file, that fresh download just picks the newest version your constraint allows, such as anything matching `~> 4.40`. That might happen to match Spacelift today. But it's luck, not a rule. When a newer azurerm release comes out, the next Spacelift run may grab it, and your DEV plans drift apart again. Also, Spacelift usually starts each run with an empty workspace anyway, so deleting a folder on your laptop changes nothing there. Nothing gets written down that every run must follow.

**Why "Commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`" is better:** the committed lock file records the exact provider version `terraform init` chose. Your laptop and every Spacelift stack then use that same version until someone runs `terraform init -upgrade` and the change is reviewed.
